body:
4,248 leads. ₹16.58 each. About 20 cents.

For a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, across six campaigns. On paper, the best cost-per-lead I had ever produced.

The client stopped the campaign anyway.

Cheap leads and leads that close are two different things, and nobody tells you that when you're starting out. A lead form on Meta (Facebook and Instagram's ad platform) just means someone tapped a button and typed a phone number. It says nothing about whether they can place a 200-piece minimum order, or whether they were even looking to buy.

If you're running lead ads for a founder, check one thing before you celebrate the cost-per-lead: pull ten leads and call them yourself. Not glance at the sheet — call. Ask what they actually want to order, and how many pieces. That one call tells you more than any dashboard.

Cheap is easy to produce. A buyer who can place the order is the only number that pays rent.

I still run an audit like this for a few brands a month, free, if you want a second pair of eyes on your leads.

#metaads #leadgen #d2c

slides.text: 4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each. Client stopped it.
Cheap leads can quietly bankrupt the follow-up team chasing them.
This was for a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, across six Meta campaigns.
₹16.58 is about 20 cents. Lowest cost-per-lead I had ever hit.
A lead form just means someone typed a phone number in. Nothing more.
It doesn't tell you if they can place a 200-piece minimum order.
So the client called the leads himself. What he heard changed everything.
Most hadn't placed a wholesale order in their life. Some barely knew what they'd clicked.
Compare: 19 UK wholesale buyers, 200-piece minimum, under $6 an enquiry. Slower, pricier, real.
Cheap leads were the good campaign. Real buyers were the good business.
Before you celebrate a low cost-per-lead, call ten of them yourself.
